newsitem.title: INDIA: Miss World stokes memories of grim Indian rite.
newsitem.headline: Miss World stokes memories of grim Indian rite.

text.p: Hindu purists' and women's groups's rage at the Miss World pageant being staged in India has stoked memories of an ancient practice of burning oneself alive as an extreme form of protest or grief.
An ally of Kinay Narayana Shashikala, the woman behind a mass suicide threat to spoil the Miss World show in the southern city of Bangalore on Saturday, defended the human torch protest.
"In India women value honour first. Life is secondary," said Pramila Nesargi, a Bangalore-based right-wing Hindu nationalist deputy in Karnataka state legislature.
"Self immolation is the biggest sacrifice women can make to save their diginity and this message will reach all corners of the world," said Nesargi.
Chaya Asarpota, a psychiatrist, said the practice of self-immolation as an extreme form of protest and sacrifice had its roots in Hindu mythology and religion.
"It's an emotional blackmail and gives one a sense of self-glorification," Asarpota said.
Last week one man in the southern state Tamil Nadu, where self-immolation is most common, set himself ablaze in a lone protest against the beauty pageant.
He died, but usually onlookers rush to put out the flames and the protester is saved.
Shashikala's militant traditionalist women's group has threatened multiple human torch protests in Bangalore's Chinnaswamy cricket stadium, the venue for Saturday's international beauty festival.
They say the show is an affront to both women and the culture in India, where Hindu temple architecture celebrates sex as a form of divine art.
"Religious beliefs give some sort of divine sanction. These are also embedded in one's sub-conscious mind," Asarpota said.

Asarpota said the practice of women committing self-immolation as an extreme form of protest could be traced to the ancient tradition of "Sati", according to which Hindu widows burned themselves on their husband's funeral pyres.
The British banned the practice of Sati, or Suttee as it was known during the days of their colonial rule.

But just two months ago, around 5,000 people in the north west desert state of Rajasthan watched a 19-year-old widow die on her husband's funeral pyre. Three of her husband's relatives were subsequently acquitted of abetting her suicide.
Legend has it that Sati, consort of Hindu god of destruction Shiva, humiliated by her father King Daksha because of his anger against her husband, burned herself to death.
"Purification by fire has always been a Hindu tradition," Asarpota said.
In recent times, self-immolation has become a form of political protest as well as an expression of grief.
In Tamil Nadu in 1965, a man burnt himself to death in protest against government moves to impose Hindi as India's official language, becoming a martyr for a local Dravidian party.
In 1987, around 30 people died from self-immolation in grief at the death of Tamil Nadu's Chief Minister M.G. Ramachandran, a former matinee idol.
And in 1990, scores of Hindu high caste students, including women, burned themselves to death to protest a government decision to reserve more state jobs to low caste candidates.
